solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Restaurant takes off, having offered "Unlimited Sushi" evenings at first

indicators.note: 'off' as in gone off or set off: TAKES rearranged
take the opening letter of each of the five words before it

parts.note: first letters of Having Offered Unlimited Sushi Evenings

explanation.surface: A restaurant's all-you-can-eat sushi nights are such a hit that business takes off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes off' reads as a single phrase meaning 'booms'; split it and 'off' is the anagram signal working on 'takes'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a restaurant whose menu is built around grilled beef.

clue.text: Smooth, very pink paper

parts.note: the Financial Times is printed on pink paper

explanation.surface: A description of some sheets of smooth, bright pink paper.
explanation.walkthrough: This is an FT puzzle, so 'pink paper' is the setter's own newspaper, the Financial Times, famous for its salmon-pink pages.
explanation.definitionFit: Soft and smooth both describe a surface pleasant to the touch.

clue.text: Rude content of book collection stolen by Heather

indicators.note: what is stolen ends up inside the thief

parts.note: Erica is the botanical name for heather
OT = Old Testament, a collection of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: Someone called Heather has pinched the saucy material from a library.
explanation.walkthrough: Heather looks like a woman's name; it is the plant, whose Latin name Erica houses OT.
explanation.definitionFit: Erotica is sexually explicit material, rude content in print or picture.

clue.text: School is more generous with info about creative work

parts.note: gen is British slang for information

explanation.surface: A school is being praised for sharing more information about its art projects.
explanation.walkthrough: GEN is informal British English for information ('get the gen'), so KINDER + G(ART)EN.
explanation.definitionFit: A kindergarten is a school for very young children.

clue.text: Obvious single suggestion

explanation.surface: An idea put forward that is plainly the only one on offer.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as adjective-adjective-noun; the first two words are the wordplay and the definition waits at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: An overtone is a subtle suggestion or implication beneath what is said.

clue.text: Small pieces of fruit and bits of green veg?

parts.note: S = small, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: A shopping list or recipe calling for fruit chunks and green vegetable scraps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small pieces of fruit' reads as one idea, but 'Small' is only S; the question mark covers defining asparagus by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Spears are the stems of asparagus or broccoli, pieces of green vegetable.

clue.text: Complain about supposedly socially acceptable way of talking

parts.words: supposedly socially acceptable way of talking

explanation.surface: Someone moans about the posh accent that is meant to sound respectable.
explanation.walkthrough: Received Pronunciation is the 'standard' upper-middle-class British accent, long treated as the socially acceptable way to speak.
explanation.definitionFit: To carp is to complain, especially about trivial things.

clue.text: Hail before storm is nothing special

explanation.surface: A weather report shrugs off a hailstorm as unremarkable.
explanation.walkthrough: Hail looks like the weather; it is the greeting, AVE.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something middling, ordinary, run-of-the-mill, is nothing special.

clue.text: Strict bonds for flats and houses, perhaps

parts.note: proper = strict, as in 'in the proper sense'

explanation.surface: Tight mortgage terms or covenants imposed on flats and houses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bonds' suggests finance next to 'flats and houses', but here it is just TIES; 'perhaps' marks flats and houses as examples.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example, marked by 'perhaps': flats and houses are two kinds of buildings people own.

clue.text: Flailed around and sank crossing lake

explanation.surface: A swimmer thrashed about and went under while trying to get across a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: F(L)OUNDERED: the two verbs differ by one letter, and the lake supplies it.
explanation.definitionFit: To flounder is to flail around clumsily.

clue.text: Showcase made money to some extent

indicators.note: only part of 'made money' is used

explanation.surface: An exhibition turned a modest profit.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters straddle the gap between the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal short form of demonstration: an event or recording that shows off a product or band.

clue.text: Intensely enjoy vintage footwear?

explanation.surface: Someone who loves wearing second-hand shoes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like old boots' is a British informal intensifier, as in 'it hit me like old boots'; the question mark flags that the phrase is being read literally.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'like old boots' means intensely or with great energy.

clue.text: Family alliances periodically ignored

indicators.note: every other letter is dropped at regular intervals, keeping the even ones

explanation.surface: Marriage ties between clans are occasionally overlooked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Family alliances' reads as one phrase, but 'Family' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A line is a family descent, as in 'the royal line'.

clue.text: Period of time at home had to end

parts.note: a term is a period of time

explanation.surface: A spell of time spent at home had to come to a close, as after lockdown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Had to end' reads as one phrase of obligation; 'had' belongs to the wordplay as ATE and 'to' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, slightly formal: to bring a contract, a pregnancy or a process to a close.

clue.text: Our fathers worked beyond closing time

indicators.note: the letters are worked into a new shape

explanation.surface: Our dads put in long hours after the shop shut.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the Lord's Prayer ('Our Father') or dutiful ancestors; it is simply ten letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: After-hours describes something happening after normal closing time.

clue.text: Female falling behind and becoming tired

explanation.surface: A woman runner drops back as she tires.
explanation.walkthrough: Wordplay and definition sit side by side and both describe a tiring runner.
explanation.definitionFit: Flagging means losing energy, becoming tired.

clue.text: That chap is in ultimate command

explanation.surface: A man is in overall charge.
explanation.walkthrough: BE(HE)ST: 'ultimate command' reads as one phrase; only 'command' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A literary synonym, now mostly heard in the phrase 'at someone's ___', meaning on their orders.

clue.text: In great health, or OK

definitions.meaning: the answer to 'How are you?' from someone thriving
OK as grudging assent, a two-word way of saying 'all right then'

explanation.surface: Someone asked how they are answers that they are fine.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is the grudging assent: 'Very well, you can go.'
explanation.definitionFit: Very well means both healthy and, as an interjection, all right.

clue.text: Domain of elected official in Ireland

parts.note: Eire is the Irish name for Ireland

explanation.surface: The constituency of an Irish politician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Domain of' reads as the patch an official controls; 'Domain' alone is the definition, and Eire is the country's Irish-language name.
explanation.definitionFit: An empire is a domain, the realm someone rules.

clue.text: Exemplar of power somewhere in ancient Europe

parts.note: Aragon was a medieval kingdom in Spain

explanation.surface: A model of might from an old European realm.
explanation.walkthrough: Aragon was an independent kingdom before uniting with Castile; it survives as a region of Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a model of excellence, the perfect example others are measured against.

clue.text: Rent facilities close to here for free?

indicators.note: the close of 'here' is its final letter

explanation.surface: A notice asks whether the nearby toilets can be hired or used for nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Facilities' is the polite word for toilets; loo is the everyday British word.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrasal verb for releasing, like unleashing a dog; 'free' is the verb here, not 'costing nothing'.

clue.text: Instrument in middle of frame beneath old vehicle

explanation.surface: A musical instrument wedged in the chassis under a vintage car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like a container signal, but it is used literally; 'beneath' only works because this is a down clue, so the later pieces sit lower in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: An ocarina is a small egg-shaped wind instrument.

clue.text: Stick around, then make oneself scarce

parts.note: to make oneself scarce = to leave

explanation.surface: Advice to hang about for a while and then slip away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick around' reads as one phrase; split it and 'Stick' is the definition. Cleave also means split, but here it is the older sense of cling.
explanation.definitionFit: An old, Biblical sense ('a man shall ___ unto his wife'): to cling fast; the word also means its opposite, to split.

clue.text: High jinks in stage adaptation of Seabiscuit?

definitions.meaning: Seabiscuit was a famous American racehorse of the 1930s; a stage version of his story is a drama about an equine

explanation.surface: Riotous fun in a theatre version of the racehorse story.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the whimsical second reading: a play about a horse.
explanation.definitionFit: Horseplay is rough, boisterous fun, high jinks.

clue.text: Attend bash?

definitions.meaning: to attend a meeting is to exist at it: split the answer into two words
bash as a verb, to hit hard

explanation.surface: An invitation: come to the party?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bash' looks like a party you might attend; it is the verb to hit. The first sense only works split as BE AT.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are plain: 'bash' is a synonym for strike, and 'attend' becomes BE AT when the answer is split.

clue.text: Clubs overwhelmed by United? Not again!

indicators.note: to be overwhelmed by something is to be swamped by it

explanation.surface: A football fan groans as Manchester United trounce the other clubs yet again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clubs' and 'United' are football, but United is ONE and Clubs is the card suit's abbreviation C.
explanation.definitionFit: Once means one time only, so not again.

clue.text: In the end, you never freaking decide to push on

indicators.note: take the end of each following word

parts.note: last letters of yoU neveR freakinG decidE

explanation.surface: An exasperated complaint about someone who can never make up their mind.
explanation.walkthrough: Four words, four last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to press or spur someone forward.

clue.text: Scot in Iceland on a mobile

indicators.note: the letters are free to move

explanation.surface: A Scotsman in Iceland chatting on his mobile phone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mobile' looks like a phone; it is the anagram signal. Caledonia is the Latin name for Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: A Caledonian is a Scot, from Caledonia, the old name for Scotland.

clue.text: Function of e.g. neon display in an auditorium

indicators.note: an auditorium is where things are heard

parts.note: a neon display is an example of a sign

explanation.surface: The purpose of a neon display in a theatre, such as an exit notice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Function' reads as purpose; it is the trigonometric function.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: one of the basic trigonometric functions, alongside cosine and tangent.

clue.text: What some agents promote in relation to almost every type of car

parts.note: re = in relation to, as in memo headers
ALL = every, minus its last letter
an estate is a British name for a station wagon

explanation.surface: Salespeople pushing nearly every kind of car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Agents' suggests car dealers; they are estate agents, who sell property.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: property agents, called realtors in the US, market land and buildings.
